The big rosters crawl. A sheet with a few hundred names spends its afternoon
on round trips to the database; sixteen names should cost what four do,
whether the sheet is taken or turned down. Reads may still scale. A rejected
roster notifies people anyway, about access they never got. And a sheet naming
a level nobody has heard of blows up halfway through instead of being turned
down like any other bad row.

the shape of its result.

class Book::AccessImport
  Result = Struct.new(:accesses, :duplicate_index)

  def initialize(book, grants)
    @book, @grants = book, grants
  end

  def import
    accesses = []
    duplicate_index = nil

    Access.transaction do
      @grants.each_with_index do |grant, index|
        access = @book.accesses.create!(user_id: grant[:user_id], level: grant[:level])
        Book::AccessNotificationJob.perform_later(access)
        accesses << access
      rescue ActiveRecord::RecordNotUnique
        duplicate_index = index
        raise ActiveRecord::Rollback
      end
    end

    duplicate_index ? Result.new([], duplicate_index) : Result.new(accesses, nil)
  end
end
=== access.rb ===
class Access < ApplicationRecord
  enum :level, %w[ reader editor ].index_by(&:itself)

  belongs_to :user
  belongs_to :book
end
=== accessable.rb ===
module Book::Accessable
  extend ActiveSupport::Concern

  included do
    has_many :accesses, dependent: :destroy
    scope :with_everyone_access, -> { where(everyone_access: true) }
  end

  class_methods do
    def accessable_or_published(user: Current.user)
      if user.present?
        accessable_or_published_books
      else
        published
      end
    end

    def accessable_or_published_books(user: Current.user)
      user.books.or(published).distinct
    end
  end

  def accessable?(user: Current.user)
    accesses.exists?(user: user)
  end

  def editable?(user: Current.user)
    access_for(user: user)&.editor? || user&.administrator?
  end

  def access_for(user: Current.user)
    accesses.find_by(user: user)
  end

  def update_access(editors:, readers:)
    editors = Set.new(editors)
    readers = Set.new(everyone_access? ? User.active.ids : readers)

    all = editors + readers
    all_accesses = all.collect { |user_id|
      { user_id: user_id, level: editors.include?(user_id) ? :editor : :reader }
    }

    accesses.upsert_all(all_accesses, unique_by: [ :book_id, :user_id ])
    accesses.where.not(user_id: all).delete_all
  end
end

class User < ApplicationRecord
  include Role, Transferable

  has_many :sessions, dependent: :destroy
  has_secure_password validations: false

  has_many :accesses, dependent: :destroy
  has_many :books, through: :accesses
  has_many :leaves, through: :books

  after_create :grant_access_to_everyone_books

  scope :active, -> { where(active: true) }
  scope :ordered, -> { order(:name) }

  def current?
    self == Current.user
  end

  def deactivate
    transaction do

      update! active: false, email_address: deactived_email_address
    end
  end

      email_address&.gsub(/@/, "-deactivated-#{SecureRandom.uuid}@")

require "test_helper"

class Book::AccessableTest < ActiveSupport::TestCase
  test "update_access always grants read access to everyone when everyone_access is set" do
    book = Book.create!(title: "My new book")
    book.update_access(editors: [], readers: [])

    assert book.everyone_access?

    User.all.each do |user|
      assert book.accessable?(user: user)
      assert_not book.editable?(user: user) unless user.administrator?
    end
  end

  test "update_access updates existing access" do
    book = Book.create!(title: "My new book", everyone_access: false)

    book.update_access(editors: [ users(:kevin).id ], readers: [])
    assert book.editable?(user: users(:kevin))

    book.update_access(editors: [], readers: [ users(:kevin).id ])
    assert book.accessable?(user: users(:kevin))
    assert_not book.editable?(user: users(:kevin))
  end

  test "update_access removes stale accesses" do
    book = Book.create!(title: "My new book", everyone_access: false)

    book.update_access(editors: [ users(:kevin).id ], readers: [ users(:jz).id ])
    assert_equal 2, book.accesses.size

    book.update_access(editors: [ users(:kevin).id ], readers: [])
    assert_equal 1, book.accesses.size
  end
end

This suggests a need for O(1) write operations regardless of the number of entries, which strongly implies a bulk insert strategy. The phrase "Reads may still scale" is critical. It *doesn't* mean read performance doesn't matter; it means we can optimize writes (bulk insert) *even if* individual record validation and user lookups add more reads which would otherwise scale (or O(n) validation). We might also get faster reads. The current implementation is painfully slow, performing a database round trip for each grant due to `create!`. This is not acceptable. **Second**, we need to fix the notification issue. The `Book::AccessNotificationJob` is currently enqueued *within* the transaction block. This means even if the transaction rolls back due to a duplicate or invalid entry, the notification job might still run, notifying users of access they never received. This is a crucial data consistency problem, and we need to ensure the notification only happens *after* the access is successfully granted and the transaction commits. We need to check Rails 8.2's `enqueue_after_transaction_commit` behavior! We also need to consider transactional tests. RAILS_ENV=test bin/rails runner '
Access.transaction do
  book = Book.create!(title: "Temp", everyone_access: false)
  user = User.create!(name: "TempU", email_address: "temp@example.com", role: :member)

  puts "--- Test 1: Access.new with unknown level ---"
  begin
    a = Access.new(book: book, user_id: user.id, level: "bogus")
    puts "No error on new: #{a.inspect}, valid?: #{a.valid?}, errors: #{a.errors.full_messages}"
  rescue => e
    puts "Raised #{e.class}: #{e.message}"
  end

  puts "--- Test 2: Access.new with nil level ---"
  begin
    a = Access.new(book: book, user_id: user.id, level: nil)
    puts "No error on new: #{a.inspect}, valid?: #{a.valid?}, errors: #{a.errors.full_messages}"
  rescue => e
    puts "Raised #{e.class}: #{e.message}"
  end

  puts "--- Test 3: Access.new with nonexistent user_id ---"
  begin
    a = Access.new(book: book, user_id: 999999, level: "reader")
    puts "No error on new: #{a.inspect}, valid?: #{a.valid?}, errors: #{a.errors.full_messages}"
  rescue => e
    puts "Raised #{e.class}: #{e.message}"
  end

  puts "--- Test 4: insert_all! with unknown level ---"
  Access.transaction(requires_new: true) do
    begin
      res = book.accesses.insert_all!([{ user_id: user.id, level: "bogus" }], returning: %w[id user_id book_id level created_at updated_at])
      puts "insert_all! succeeded: #{res.to_a.inspect}"
    rescue => e
      puts "insert_all! raised #{e.class}: #{e.message}"
    end
    raise ActiveRecord::Rollback
  end

  puts "--- Test 5: insert_all! with nonexistent user_id ---"
  Access.transaction(requires_new: true) do
    begin
      res = book.accesses.insert_all!([{ user_id: 999999, level: "reader" }])
      puts "insert_all! succeeded: #{res.to_a.inspect}"
    rescue => e
      puts "insert_all! raised #{e.class}: #{e.message}"
    end
    raise ActiveRecord::Rollback
  end

  raise ActiveRecord::Rollback
end
'

Okay, wow, this is quite a puzzle! After reviewing the tests and the prompt again, a few critical things have become crystal clear. The tests point to a crucial understanding of how `enum` validations and database interactions are working, and the prompt's wording is packed with important hints about performance and error handling.

First, the original implementation seems to have a significant performance bottleneck. The problem likely stems from the fact that we're using individual `.create!` calls within a loop inside a transaction. This likely triggers a database query for each row during the validation process, and the `belongs_to :user` association means there will be at least one `SELECT` per row. "Reads may still scale" must be about these queries, since we know writes are the slow part!

The `enum` validation, interestingly, doesn't throw an `ArgumentError` when using `enum` – it's actually handled by Rails. If the `validate: true` option on the enum is set, it will flag the record as invalid and throw an `ActiveRecord::RecordInvalid` instead of the more general `ArgumentError` and a different result than a duplicate. This tells us what should happen when a level isn't recognized!

Now, the core of the problem lies in the error handling and the structure of `Book::AccessImport`. The original code throws an exception halfway through if a bad row is encountered (specifically, due to an invalid `user_id` or `level`). This is inconsistent with how duplicate rows are handled. Specifically, the prompt specifies this behavior! The prompt wants to ensure that bad rows "turn down like any other bad row."

So the prompt clearly wants the result to be consistent, no matter what went wrong. The `duplicate_index` can clearly be set to the row that failed, so we should return something that says which row it happened on, so everything that happens is clear to the user.

Thus, the key is to perform validation in a batch, and return information to the user when a row fails, like a normal error condition.

Let's find the best way to do so!

module ActiveJob
  module EnqueueAfterTransactionCommit # :nodoc:
    class << self
      def included(base)
        ActiveJob.singleton_class.prepend(ActiveJobMethods)
      end
    end

    module ActiveJobMethods
      # Ensures perform_all_later respects each job's enqueue_after_transaction_commit configuration.
      # Jobs with enqueue_after_transaction_commit set to true are deferred and enqueued only after the transaction commits;
      # other jobs are enqueued immediately. This ensures enqueuing timing matches the per-job setting.
      def perform_all_later(*jobs)
        jobs.flatten!
        deferred_jobs, immediate_jobs = jobs.partition { |job| job.class.enqueue_after_transaction_commit }
        super(immediate_jobs) if immediate_jobs.any?
        ActiveRecord.after_all_transactions_commit { super(deferred_jobs) } if deferred_jobs.any?
        nil
      end
    end

    private
      def raw_enqueue
        if self.class.enqueue_after_transaction_commit
          self.successfully_enqueued = true
          ActiveRecord.after_all_transactions_commit do
            self.successfully_enqueued = false
            super
          end
          self
        else
          super
        end
      end
  end
end

The key is to address the performance hit and incorrect behaviors while preserving the existing entry point and the shape of the result, `Result = Struct.new(:accesses, :duplicate_index)`.

Let's break down the issues one by one.

Complaint 1: Big rosters are slow. We have N+1 writes. When sixteen names cost the same as four, it means one, not N, writes.

Complaint 2: Rejected rosters notify users. We have no mechanism for checking if a row *should* be notified *before* the notification runs. If we're going to use `AccessNotificationJob`, we need an option to *not* notify a row.

Complaint 3: "A sheet naming a level nobody has heard of blows up halfway through instead of being turned down like any other bad row." This is the most crucial, and it hints that our current exception handling is inconsistent.

The current code's behavior for different "bad rows" is as follows:

| Bad Row Type                      | Behavior                                                                                                             | Exception                                                                             |
| :-------------------------------- | :------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| Duplicate `user_id`              |  Inserts previous rows, then encounters a duplicate. Transaction rolls back. `duplicate_index` is set.               | `ActiveRecord::RecordNotUnique` (rescued) -> Return `Result.new([], index)`          |
| Nonexistent `user_id`             | Inserts previous rows, validation fails. Transaction rolls back.                                                     | `ActiveRecord::RecordInvalid`                                                        |
| `level: nil` or `level: ""`       | Inserts previous rows, DB constraint fails. Transaction rolls back.                                                   | `ActiveRecord::NotNullViolation`                                                       |
| Unknown `level` (`"admin"`, etc.) | Inserts previous rows, `enum` setter raises an error. Transaction rolls back. Jobs for previous rows may have enqueued | `ArgumentError: 'admin' is not a valid level`                                       |

The phrase "turned down like any other bad row" is the key to fixing our problem. Right now, a bad `level` (and a bad `user_id` and a `nil` `level`) behaves *differently* than our code expects because an invalid `level` raises an `ArgumentError` *and* an `ActiveRecord::NotNullViolation`.

The *current* `Access` model is defined as:

  belongs_to :user
  belongs_to :book
end

In Rails 7.1+, `enum :level, %w[ reader editor ].index_by(&:itself), validate: true` *should* be added to fix exactly what the prompt is describing: when the *database* is not what we expect and there is an *application* issue, the application should throw `ActiveRecord::RecordInvalid` so that the application has a consistent mechanism for handling all invalid data.

Here is the plan:

2.  Pre-validate the roster before attempting database inserts. If ANY validation fails, the whole import fails (with *no* database writes) and *no* notifications will be enqueued. This pre-validation is key to fixing the N+1 problem.

The implications are that "sixteen names cost what four do" because there will be either *zero* writes if the roster is invalid or *one* set of writes if the roster is valid. We also now address the problem of notifying users who are not granted access.

class Book::AccessImport
  Result = Struct.new(:accesses, :duplicate_index)

  def initialize(book, grants)
    @book, @grants = book, grants
  end

  def import
    grants = @grants.to_a
    return Result.new([], nil) if grants.empty?

    records = build_records(grants)
    accesses = []
    duplicate_index = nil

    Access.transaction(requires_new: true) do
      duplicate_index = validate_and_find_duplicate(records)
      raise ActiveRecord::Rollback if duplicate_index

      accesses = bulk_insert(records)
    rescue ActiveRecord::RecordNotUnique
      duplicate_index = find_duplicate_index(records)
      raise ActiveRecord::Rollback
    end

    if duplicate_index
      Result.new([], duplicate_index)
    else
      notify(accesses)
      Result.new(accesses, nil)
    end
  end

  private
    def build_records(grants)
      grants.map do |grant|
        Access.new(book: @book, user_id: grant[:user_id], level: grant[:level])
      end
    end

    def validate_and_find_duplicate(records)
      user_ids = records.filter_map(&:user_id).uniq
      users_by_id = User.where(id: user_ids).index_by(&:id)
      seen_user_ids = existing_user_ids_for(user_ids)

      records.each_with_index do |record, index|
        if (user = users_by_id[record.user_id])
          record.user = user
        end

        record.validate!

        return index unless seen_user_ids.add?(record.user_id)
      end

      nil
    end

    def find_duplicate_index(records)
      seen_user_ids = existing_user_ids_for(records.filter_map(&:user_id).uniq)
      records.index { |record| !seen_user_ids.add?(record.user_id) }
    end

    def existing_user_ids_for(user_ids)
      @book.accesses.where(user_id: user_ids).pluck(:user_id).to_set
    end

    def bulk_insert(records)
      rows = records.map { |record| { user_id: record.user_id, level: record.level } }
      ids = @book.accesses.insert_all!(rows, returning: :id).rows.flatten
      accesses_by_user_id = @book.accesses.where(id: ids).index_by(&:user_id)
      records.map { |record| accesses_by_user_id.fetch(record.user_id) }
    end

    def notify(accesses)
      accesses.each { |access| Book::AccessNotificationJob.perform_later(access) }
    end
end
EOF

class Book::AccessImport
  Result = Struct.new(:accesses, :duplicate_index)

  def initialize(book, grants)
    @book, @grants = book, grants
  end

  def import
    grants = @grants.to_a
    return Result.new([], nil) if grants.empty?

    records = build_records(grants)
    accesses = []
    duplicate_index = nil

    Access.transaction(requires_new: true) do
      duplicate_index = validate_and_find_duplicate(records)
      raise ActiveRecord::Rollback if duplicate_index

      accesses = bulk_insert(records)
    rescue ActiveRecord::RecordNotUnique
      duplicate_index = find_duplicate_index(records)
      raise unless duplicate_index
      raise ActiveRecord::Rollback
    end

    if duplicate_index
      Result.new([], duplicate_index)
    else
      notify(accesses)
      Result.new(accesses, nil)
    end
  end

  private
    def build_records(grants)
      grants.map do |grant|
        Access.new(book: @book, user_id: grant[:user_id], level: grant[:level])
      end
    end

    def validate_and_find_duplicate(records)
      user_ids = records.filter_map(&:user_id).uniq
      users_by_id = User.where(id: user_ids).index_by(&:id)
      seen_user_ids = existing_user_ids_for(user_ids)

      records.each_with_index do |record, index|
        if (user = users_by_id[record.user_id])
          record.user = user
        end

        record.validate!

        return index unless seen_user_ids.add?(record.user_id)
      end

      nil
    end

    def find_duplicate_index(records)
      seen_user_ids = existing_user_ids_for(records.filter_map(&:user_id).uniq)
      records.index { |record| !seen_user_ids.add?(record.user_id) }
    end

    def existing_user_ids_for(user_ids)
      @book.accesses.where(user_id: user_ids).pluck(:user_id).to_set
    end

    def bulk_insert(records)
      rows = records.map { |record| { user_id: record.user_id, level: record.level } }
      ids = @book.accesses.insert_all!(rows, returning: :id).rows.flatten
      accesses_by_user_id = @book.accesses.where(id: ids).index_by(&:user_id)
      records.map { |record| accesses_by_user_id.fetch(record.user_id) }
    end

    def notify(accesses)
      accesses.each { |access| Book::AccessNotificationJob.perform_later(access) }
    end

    def count_sql
      queries = []
      callback = ->(*, payload) do
        next if payload[:name] == "SCHEMA"
        sql = payload[:sql]
        queries << sql unless sql.match?(/\A\s*(BEGIN|COMMIT|ROLLBACK|SAVEPOINT|RELEASE)/i)

      ActiveSupport::Notifications.subscribed(callback, "sql.active_record") do
        yield
      end

      writes = queries.count { |sql| sql.match?(/\A\s*(INSERT|UPDATE|DELETE)/i) }
      reads = queries.count { |sql| sql.match?(/\A\s*SELECT/i) }
      [ writes, reads ]
    end
